strengths: The core idea of exploiting information asymmetry (subtasks are easy to generate/verify but hard when composed) is a clean, well-motivated mechanism for producing scalable, difficulty-controllable benchmarks without human annotation.

Extensive validation of the automatic verifier: human agreement study (Table 1), calibration curves against human-judged completion scores across difficulty levels (Fig. 2), and an adversarial stress test with near-miss vs. benign perturbations (Table 2), which meaningfully addresses known concerns about LLM-based judges (Lu et al., 2025).

Thorough ablations beyond the main benchmark: comparison against a direct-instruction baseline isolating the effect of information asymmetry (Table 5), sensitivity analysis to the choice of base generator model (Table 6), and evaluation with multiple agent scaffolds (bare LLM, Agent S2.5, Agent S3) across several backbones (o4-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.1).
Strong cost/scalability argument with a transparent cost breakdown ($0.6/trajectory, $0.1/task) compared against realistic human-annotation cost estimates for τ-bench, OSWorld, and TheAgentCompany.
Generality demonstrated by porting the pipeline to a second, structurally different environment (InSTA web agent), showing the same qualitative difficulty-scaling trend.

Good reproducibility support: full prompt templates for all six agent roles, action-space statistics, and detailed dataset statistics (horizon, app count, switches, memory span) that substantiate the difficulty-scaling claims.

Clear empirical result showing steep performance degradation of SOTA multimodal LLM agents with increasing task difficulty, and a large human-vs-agent performance gap (70% vs <20%), demonstrating discriminative power of the benchmark.
weaknesses: The paper's stated motivation includes both training and evaluating agents, but no experiments show the generated data actually improves agent training/fine-tuning performance downstream; the contribution is essentially an automatically-generated benchmark rather than a demonstrated data-generation-for-training pipeline.

The same automatic verifier is used both to filter/accept subtasks during data generation and to score agent success during evaluation, creating a potential circularity that could bias reported success rates in ways not fully disentangled by the (still limited, ~100-sample) human validation study.

Task difficulty is controlled essentially through a single knob (number of chained subtasks/horizon); other complexity axes (e.g., fine-grained visual discrimination) are measured but not directly manipulated, and the paper does not analyze whether performance drops are driven by genuine reasoning/planning difficulty vs. compounding low-level GUI grounding errors (which the failure-mode analysis suggests may dominate).

Persona-conditioned generation and LLM summarization may introduce systematic artifacts or reduce genuine semantic diversity; diversity claims rely mainly on surface statistics (app/domain distribution, token counts) rather than deeper analysis of task novelty or redundancy across the 6,000+ generated tasks.

Statistical rigor in the main results is uneven — Figure 4 (primary benchmark result) lacks confidence intervals/error bars for the reported success rates (only later figures like S3 comparisons include them), making it harder to assess significance of small differences between difficulty levels or models.

The comparison between AgentSynth and the direct-instruction baseline (Table 5) is somewhat confounded, since AgentSynth's pipeline includes revision/partial-credit mechanisms not present in the one-shot baseline, making the generation-success-rate comparison less of an apples-to-apples test of information asymmetry alone.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to related synthetic-data works cited (e.g., Learn-by-interact, OS-Genesis, AgentTrek), with the main differentiator being the specific subtask-chaining-then-summarizing mechanism rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: exploiting information asymmetry between forward generation (easy) and evaluation (hard) to synthesize long-horizon computer-use tasks that are cheap to generate but genuinely difficult to solve.

Extensive and thoughtful supporting analyses beyond the main benchmark: verifier calibration against human judgment, an adversarial stress test of the verifier (near-miss vs. benign perturbations), and human inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) on quality metrics.

Strong ablation studies that isolate the contribution of the proposed method: a direct-instruction baseline showing the asymmetry effect (flat generation success vs. steep evaluation drop for AgentSynth, vs. the opposite pattern for one-shot long-horizon generation), and robustness checks across different base generator models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5.1).
Demonstrates generality of the pipeline by applying it to a second, structurally different environment (InSTA web agent), showing consistent difficulty scaling trends.

Good evaluation breadth across multiple SOTA backbones (o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-pro, Claude-3.7, GPT-5/5.1) and multiple agent scaffolds (bare LLM, Agent S2.5, Agent S3), showing the difficulty trend is robust to scaffolding choices.
Cost-efficiency and scalability are clearly quantified and compared against several human-annotated datasets, supporting the claimed practical value of the pipeline.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support: full prompt templates, action space, and cost-accounting details are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The paper's title and framing emphasize task generation 'for generalist computer-use agents' and motivate the work partly around training data for agents, but no experiments actually show that training/fine-tuning an agent on AgentSynth trajectories improves downstream performance — the empirical contribution is essentially a benchmark plus a data-generation method, not a demonstrated training benefit.

The automatic LLM-based verifier used for pipeline construction is also used to score all model evaluations in Section 5, creating a degree of circularity; despite the calibration and adversarial stress-test analyses, an 88% agreement rate with humans (and 12% false-negative-avoidance rate under near-miss perturbations) could still meaningfully shift the already very low success-rate numbers (4-18%) reported for SOTA models.

Evaluation sample sizes are fairly small (50 tasks per difficulty level for the main benchmark, 20 tasks for the human baseline), and no confidence intervals/error bars are reported for the primary Figure 4 results, limiting the statistical strength of claims about steep performance drop-off.

Task difficulty is controlled almost exclusively via number of chained subtasks (horizon); while the paper shows other properties (apps, memory span, switches) scale together, this conflation makes it hard to disentangle whether harder levels are more challenging due to genuine reasoning complexity or simply longer execution/compounding-error exposure.

Task generation relies solely on OpenAI models (GPT-4.1 family) for the main dataset and prompts are fairly constrained (avoiding logins, emails, forms), which may bias the diversity and realism of the resulting persona-driven tasks toward a narrow style, despite the qualitative examples looking reasonable.

The comparison table (Table 4) qualitatively marks AgentSynth favorably on nearly all axes (multi-domain, scalable, long-horizon) in a somewhat self-serving binary fashion without a more nuanced discussion of any remaining limitations relative to prior benchmarks.
